name: YaFF (Yet another Flat Format)
workload: Median time to read every field out of an already-serialized buffer, for flat messages (10/100 uint64 fields) and a 3-level hierarchical message under hot (~2KB working set) and cold (~512MB working set) access patterns, using google/benchmark.
claimed_speedup: Flat Layout reads are ~25-50x faster than Protobuf and ~2-2.5x faster than FlatBuffers on flat messages (e.g. 100-field flat read: 25.99ns YaFF vs 1383.74ns Protobuf vs 54.81ns FlatBuffers); hierarchical hot access is ~25x faster than Protobuf and ~3.5x faster than FlatBuffers
compiler_and_flags: Clang 20.1.8, CMake Release build (CMake's Release default is -O3 -DNDEBUG; no -march or other extra flags in the benchmark CMakeLists), C++20; google/benchmark 1.9.5, FlatBuffers 24.12.23, Protobuf >=5.26 via Conan (the exact Protobuf version is not stated)
tradeoffs: Still requires an existing .proto schema (built as a companion physical layout for Protobuf, not a schema replacement); adds adaptive-layout complexity; C++ only today, multi-language bindings are roadmap items
caveats: Very young project (repo created 2026-04-07), first-party benchmark on a single machine (EPYC 7713, DDR4); the authors say only the ratios generalize. The Protobuf timings include ParseFromString/ParseFromArray of the whole message on every iteration, because Protobuf cannot read fields without parsing. So this compares zero-copy field access with parse-plus-access, not serialization speed. The win shrinks sharply with cold random access (~512 MB working set): 206.64 vs 387.48 ns vs Protobuf (~1.9x) and vs 300.13 ns for FlatBuffers (~1.45x). With hot hierarchical access and hand-cached access chains, FlatBuffers is only ~2.1x slower (20.89 vs 9.81 ns), not 3.5x (derived from page data). The Protobuf version is not pinned (Conan protobuf/[>=5.26]). GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the standard Apache-2.0 notice (Copyright 2026 YANDEX LLC).

name: Cista++
workload: Serialize/deserialize/traverse a graph of nodes and edges (object-oriented graph with pointers/indices) using the 'offset' and 'raw' variants of Cista++, compared to cereal, Cap'n Proto, and FlatBuffers
claimed_speedup: Cista++ `offset` (slim variant) vs cereal: serialize 4 ms vs 216 ms, deserialize 0.16 ms vs 111.00 ms, deserialize & traverse 66 ms vs 174 ms (derived from page data: ~54x, ~690x, ~2.6x); serialized size 25.3M vs 37.8M. Traverse alone is 67 ms for both. Compile time (clang-7 on Mac OS X): Cista++ `raw` 1.351 s vs cereal 1.827 s
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release from the README build steps (CMakeLists.txt adds no other optimization flags; C++20); compile-time table uses clang-7 on Mac OS X
tradeoffs: The zero-copy 'offset' variant requires reading/writing in a fixed pointer-offset layout (no relocation), so both ends must share pointer width/endianness; the 'raw' variant (native pointers, relocatable) is far slower to serialize (3555ms) because of the extra relocation pass. Not schema-evolution-friendly like protobuf/capnproto without opt-in versioning.
caveats: Benchmark numbers come from felixguendling's own companion repo (cpp-serialization-benchmark), so they are first-party, but methodology (code, compiler, build type, CPU) is public, which is why it qualifies for tier A. The run is from 2021-12-18 (benchmark_result.txt) with Cista pinned as a submodule at d3492bf; the benchmark repo has not changed since 2021-12-31, and that run warns that CPU scaling was enabled. The 1.351 s compile time is for the `raw` variant, and `raw` serializes slower than cereal (650 ms vs 216 ms); the win is for the `offset` slim variant. The main cista README shows an older 2019 run (72 ms vs 239 ms serialize), which points the same direction. The very large deserialize speedup vs cereal is an architectural effect of zero-copy access (no parsing step), not a benchmarking artifact.

tradeoffs: In-situ, destructive parser (mutates the source buffer); allocates DOM nodes from an internal per-instance pool, which becomes a scaling bottleneck at large file sizes versus newer arena/SoA designs (see libsimdxml and parshred entries, both of which cite this exact weakness); C++03-era single-header code with no active upstream maintainer since the 1.13 release (2009); canonical home is SourceForge (http://rapidxml.sourceforge.net/), this GitHub repo is a maintained third-party host of the original source
caveats: Only evidence is bemayer/xml-benchmark, a small third-party suite (1 star, no license, created 2026-04-06). It benchmarks the SourceForge rapidxml-1.13.zip, not this repo, though the parser code is the same 1.13. Its size buckets are misleading: deep-shape files are 5.6-100 MiB with up to 5,000 nesting levels. libxml2 2.9.14 (Debian bookworm) stops at depth 256 without XML_PARSE_HUGE (parser.c nodePush calls xmlHaltParser). The libxml2 bench calls xmlParseMemory without checking the result, so its deep-file times measure a halted partial parse. This favors libxml2, so the ~3.9-4.0x RapidXml win at 10MB/100MB is if anything conservative. The 'libxml2 faster at 100KB/1MB' result is probably this artifact. Per-shape numbers are not published. The run is a single monthly run on a CI runner with no CPU model. RapidXml loses to pugixml at every size, so cite only libxml2 as the beaten baseline. RapidXml is a non-validating in-situ parser, while libxml2 builds a full DOM. The upstream parser has had no release since 1.13 (header dated 2009; SourceForge last updated 2013-04-26). externpro's recent commits (last 2026-08-31) are CMake/CI packaging only, so 'active' reflects packaging, not parser development.
